resources.string: The parser has X on top and reads plus. Which rule of X does it use? FIRST and FOLLOW already know the answer.
Tap the rule the parser uses with plus in the input.
The token read is plus. Which rule starts with it?
X goes to plus T X, because that rule starts with plus.
But computing the sets at every token would be slow. The compiler computes them once and writes the answers down.
That answer sheet is the LL(1) table: one cell for each pair of nonterminal and next token.
The table recipe has three steps. You apply the first two to every rule of the grammar.
X goes to epsilon went into the closing parenthesis column. Tap the rule that did that.
Epsilon vanishes. Then what comes after X is in charge.
Exactly. Step two: a nullable rule goes into the FOLLOW columns.
Another grammar: a list of ids separated by commas. Now you fill in the table.
L goes to id R. Which cell does that rule go into? Tap.
The right-hand side starts with id. Use step one.
Row L, id column.
R goes to comma, id, R. Tap its cell.
It starts with the comma.
Its FIRST is the comma.
R also goes to epsilon. FOLLOW of R is just the dollar sign. Tap the cell.
Step two: a nullable rule goes into the FOLLOW columns.
Nice. R vanishes when the input ends.
No cell ended up with two rules. This grammar is LL(1), and the empty cells are syntax errors.
Now a case that shows up on exams. S goes to A B. There is no epsilon written, but A and B can both vanish.
Which columns does the rule S goes to A B go in? Tap all of them.
Step one: FIRST of A B. Step two: can A B vanish entirely? Then look at FOLLOW of S.
All three. The a and the b come from FIRST. A and B vanish together, so the rule also goes under dollar, the FOLLOW of S.
The rest comes out the same way. No cell has two rules, so it is LL(1). A rule with no epsilon written can still be nullable.
One more: S goes to a b, or to a c.
Which cell gets both rules of S? Tap it.
Look at the first token of each rule.
Row S, column a. Both rules start with a.
Two rules in one cell. Reading a, the parser cannot tell which to use, so it is not LL(1). Left factoring, from the Bridge, delays the choice until after the a.
1. A → α goes into the columns of FIRST(α).
2. If α is nullable, also into those of FOLLOW(A).
3. Two rules in a cell: not LL(1). Empty: error.
The parser shifted E and plus. To know whether to shift or reduce, it must remember where it is in each rule.
The stack already has E and plus. What still has to arrive to complete the rule? Tap it.
Compare the stack with the right side of the rule, left to right.
The n is missing. The parser is in the middle of the rule, right after the plus.
Without that, it cannot tell whether it still expects an n or the handle is already complete.
An LR(0) item is a rule with a dot in its right-hand side. The dot marks how far the rule has been read.
The recipe starts with an extra rule, S prime goes to S, and uses two operations.
Dot before E. Which operation pulls in the rules of E? Tap it.
It's the one that looks at the symbol right after the dot.
You got it. Closure.
After the goto, always do the closure again. Repeat for each symbol after a dot, until no new state appears.
Another grammar: parentheses around id. State zero starts with S prime goes to dot S.
In state zero, the dot is before S. Which items does the closure pull in? Tap both.
The dot sits at the start of the rules of S.
The two items with the dot at the start.
From state zero, reading id, where does the dot go? Tap the item.
The dot jumps over the id.
Dot at the end: this state reduces.
Reading an opening parenthesis, the dot lands before S. Does it need a closure?
A dot before a nonterminal always pulls in its rules.
That's it. The rules of S come in again.
The states are ready. Where there is a complete item, the table will reduce. Where the dot is before a terminal, it will shift.
The whole automaton
Repeating goto and closure until no new state appears gives six states. Below are the items of the open parenthesis state.
In that state, reading open parenthesis again, where does goto lead? Tap the state.
Move the dot over the open parenthesis and close. Compare the result with the states that already exist.
To itself. Goto gives the same set of items, and the same set is the same state. That is why the construction ends.
Which state accepts the input? Tap it.
Look for the item of the extra rule with the dot at the end.
The state of S prime goes to S dot. With dollar in the input, it accepts.
Six states. Two reduce: the id one and the closed parenthesis one. One accepts, and in the others the dot is before a symbol.
1. Closure: a dot before A pulls in the rules of A.
2. Goto: move the dot over X and close again.
3. Dot at the end: complete item, may reduce.
State zero
yes
no
This state has the complete item E goes to n, dot. LR(0) would always reduce. But is reducing now right?
In this grammar, which tokens can come right after E? Tap both.
In the rule E goes to E plus n, look at what follows the first E. Also remember that E is the start symbol.
Plus and dollar. The plus comes from the rule, and the dollar because E is the start symbol.
If the next token cannot come after E, the reduction leads to a dead end.
SLR, for Simple LR, reduces by A only when the next token is in FOLLOW of A.
The SLR table recipe has three rules.
State two has E goes to n, dot. Which rule fills its row? Tap it.
The dot is at the end of the rule.
Correct. Rule two: reduce in the FOLLOW columns.
Rule three: the item S prime goes to S, dot, accepts the input in the dollar column. And a goto on a nonterminal becomes just the state number.
Now parentheses around id. The state has S goes to id, dot.
The FOLLOW of S has closing parenthesis and dollar sign. Tap the reduce cells.
Rule two: only in the FOLLOW columns.
In the other columns, the cell stays empty.
After id, the next token is an opening parenthesis. Tap what the table does.
The opening parenthesis cell stayed empty.
An empty cell is a syntax error.
With FOLLOW, the table reduces only where the rule can end. In the practice step, you run an input with this table.
1. Goto on terminal t: s in column t.
2. A → α •: r in the columns of FOLLOW(A).
3. S' → S •: ok (accept) in the $ column.
reduce
shift
error
There are unambiguous grammars whose SLR table has a conflict. FOLLOW says reduce where it should not.
For the item E goes to n, which tokens get a reduce in the SLR table? Tap all of them.
SLR looks at the FOLLOW of E, which is on the screen.
Plus, close parenthesis and end of input. SLR reduces on every token in FOLLOW of E, and n is not there.
The problem: FOLLOW of A is a single set for the whole grammar. It does not know which state the parser is in.
The LR(1) item keeps, along with the rule and the dot, the token that can come next in that context: the lookahead.
Here are four LR(1) items. After the comma comes the lookahead. The reduction holds only if the next token is that one.
The LALR recipe has two steps.
Which step makes the table small again? Tap it.
It's the step that merges states.
Nice. Merging equal cores shrinks the table.
Since each reduction looks only at the lookaheads of its own state, LALR reduces by mistake less often than SLR.
Two LR(1) states from another grammar. Compare them.
Which two items have the same core? Tap them.
Ignore the token after the comma.
Same rule, same dot.
Merged, which lookaheads does the item get? Tap the right box.
Join the tokens of both.
Closing parenthesis and dollar sign in the same item.
That is how LALR stays the size of SLR and keeps the precision of the lookahead.
1. Build the LR(1) states, with lookahead.
2. Merge equal cores and union the lookaheads.
Result: SLR size, fewer conflicts.
This DFA has four states. Maybe two of them play exactly the same role.
Which of these states is final? Tap it.
A final state has a double circle.
D is the only final one.
Two states are equivalent when, starting from them, the same strings lead to accept and the same lead to reject.
Merging the equivalent states gives the minimal DFA: the smallest one that recognizes the same language.
The tool is the table of pairs. Each cell compares two states. An X in the cell means the two are different.
The recipe has three steps and repeats until it stops.
I marked A with B because they go to C and D. Tap the rule I used.
It wasn't because one is final. It was because of where they go.
Rule two, by destination.
Stop only when a whole round marks nothing. A new mark can cause another in the next round.
Another automaton: P, Q and R, with R final.
Tap the pairs the first rule marks.
Look for the pairs with R, which is final.
Only R is final. The other two aren't.
P and Q, on zero, both go to Q. On one, to R. Merge or split?
The destinations are the same. No marked pair shows up.
Correct. The two become a single state.
Two states are left. The automaton recognizes the same language as before.
The book DFA
Now the DFA from the book, which ends in a b b. Only E is final. In each cell, I write the round of the mark.
Round one: E, which is final, with all the others.
Round two. Which pairs go, on b, to a pair with E? Tap them.
Only D goes to E on b. The others go to C or to D.
D with A, B and C. On b, D goes to E, and the others do not.
Round three. I marked round two with the number two. Which blank cells fall now? Tap them.
On b, A goes to C, and B goes to D. The pair C and D fell in round two.
A with B and B with C. Both fall because of a mark from round two.
One mark pulled another. That is why the recipe repeats: stopping at round two would leave these pairs blank.
In round four, nothing changes. Which cell stayed blank? Tap it.
Look for the cell with no number.
A with C. On a, both go to B. On b, both go to C.
A and C become a single state. The minimal DFA has four states, as in the book.
One more: a star b star. After b, reading a has no way back. The arrow goes to the dead state M. To minimize, it has to appear.
Round one: which pairs does the first rule mark? Tap them.
P and Q are final. The dead state is not.
P with M and Q with M. The dead state is a non-final state like any other.
And P with Q? On a, P goes to P, and Q goes to M. Merge or separate?
The pair P and M is already marked.
Separate. P and M are different, so P and Q are too. Without the dead state in the table, they would look equal, and the DFA would accept b a.
merge
split
1. Mark every final with non-final pair.
2. Mark the pair that goes to a marked pair.
3. Repeat until nothing changes. Blank: merge.
The parser built the parse tree. It has a node for each rule used, and it gets huge.
Of these five pieces, which ones change the result? Tap them.
Remove the parentheses. Does the result change?
The a, the plus and the b. The parentheses around b change nothing.
The following phases only need to know which operation it is and which the operands are.
The tree that keeps only that is the abstract syntax tree, the AST.
The recipe for building the AST has three rules.
In the tree, each name became a leaf. Which rule is that? Tap it.
A name has no children.
Exactly. Rule two: values and names become leaves.
Rule three: the parenthesis was only there to group. In the AST, the shape of the tree itself shows the grouping.
Now build the AST for total times, open parenthesis, price minus two.
Which operator goes at the root? Tap it.
The parenthesis makes the minus happen first. Whatever comes last is the root.
Times is the last operation, so it goes at the root.
The minus sits under the times. What are the minus's children? Tap them.
They're the two sides of the minus.
Price and two are leaves of the minus.
No parentheses in the tree, and the order is still right: whatever sits deeper is computed first.
1. An operator becomes a node; operands become children.
2. A value or a name becomes a leaf.
3. Parentheses and pass-through rules vanish.
The processor knows nothing about variables. It only knows registers, which are few and fast, and memory locations.
The operation total plus one is about to happen. Where can it be done? Tap all of them.
The operation happens inside the processor. The orange boxes live there.
In dollar t zero or dollar t one. That is why lw first brings total from memory into a register.
Math only happens between registers, inside the processor.
Code generation translates each three-address line into machine instructions. Here the machine is MIPS.
The recipe for each three-address line has three steps.
Which step brings the values from memory? Tap it.
The processor only adds what's already in a register.
You got it. The lw comes first.
Step three: without the sw, the result stays only in the register and is lost when it is reused.
Now price plus tax. The lines are out of order.
Tap the two lines that come first.
Before adding, the values have to be in registers.
The two lw's open the trio.
And which line closes the trio? Tap it.
The result has to go back to memory.
The sw stores the result.
Now you can translate any three-address line into MIPS: two lw, the operation and one sw.
1. lw: load each operand into a register.
2. Math between registers: add, sub, mul.
3. sw: store the result in memory.
